notable_claims: Users own the information in their disk files regardless of who owns the physical disk.
Email should be treated as private communication.
Warrants must be obtained prior to searches of computer systems.
Computer and network access should not be denied without due process.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie proposes a framework for academic freedoms as applied to computers. He categorizes these rights into freedom of expression, privacy, due process, access, and resource limits. The proposal seeks to establish standards for user ownership of data and protections against arbitrary denial of network access.
classification.title: Which rights?

notable_claims: The conflict represents a shift from individual 'flame wars' to organized efforts by network collectives to trigger administrative censorship.
System managers may use 'inappropriate use of computer resources' as a justification to silence controversial groups.
classification.summary: Stan Kulikowski II discusses a conflict between the 'legs' list and the 'educom-w' group regarding the appropriateness of a list dedicated to images of women's legs. He frames this as a case study in computer freedom, noting that members of one collective are attempting to pressure system management to silence another group by citing 'inappropriate use of computer resources.'
classification.title: leggo my eggo

notable_claims: The EFF hosted an electronic library specifically dedicated to computers and academic freedom.
University computer policies from numerous institutions were systematically collected via the Computer Underground Digest archives.
Professor John McCarthy led a campaign to restore 'rec.humor.funny' at Stanford University after it was suppressed in 1989.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie announces that back issues of CAF-news and a collection of university computer policy statements are available via anonymous FTP from eff.org. The archive includes materials on email privacy, the Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986, and documentation regarding censorship of 'rec.humor.funny' at Stanford University.
classification.title: New to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) archive

identity.subject: New to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) archive

notable_claims: General principles of academic freedom should apply to every aspect of the university, including computers and networks.
Broad policy provisions (like those at Case Western) may be insufficient to prevent censorship without specific enumerations of rights.
System administrators should advocate for computer rights similarly to how librarians advocate for the freedom to read.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the challenges of defining specific academic freedom rights for computers and networks. He debates whether a broad application of general academic freedom principles is sufficient or if explicit enumerations are necessary to prevent censorship. He also considers how resource scarcity in university computing environments might impact the implementation of these rights.
classification.title: Re: Which rights?

notable_claims: Incremental costs should not be used as a pretext for content-based censorship of electronic communications.
The right to use university resources for expression is tied to the principles of academic freedom and tuition/employment.
Limiting access based on data volume (e.g., disk space) is more legitimate than limiting access based on content categories.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that access to electronic mail and newsgroups should be viewed as a benefit of university membership and protected from content-based censorship. He contrasts the legitimacy of restricting resources based on technical costs (e.g., disk space) versus restricting them based on the nature of the content. The discussion references established academic freedom standards, including those from the American Library Association.
classification.title: Which Rights?

notable_claims: Information in a user's disk files should be considered private regardless of who owns the hardware.
University officials generally require warrants or specific authorizations to search offices or residence halls.
Public university employees maintain constitutional privacy rights that protect against warrantless searches of their desks.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that privacy rights for electronic files should be analogous to the privacy of physical desks and offices. He cites university student codes and ACLU guidance on Fourth Amendment rights to argue against the notion that public university employees forfeit all privacy regarding their work documents.
classification.title: RE: Which rights?

notable_claims: Censoring notes, searching disk files, and removing computer/network access are viewed by students and faculty as serious penalties.
Due process in academic settings should include written notice of charges, the right to an adviser, and a hearing before a committee of faculty or students.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that actions such as censoring notes, searching disk files, and revoking computer or network access constitute serious penalties requiring due process. He references the 'Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students' to define procedural standards for disciplinary hearings and conduct regulations in an academic setting.
classification.title: RE: Which rights?

notable_claims: Commercial use of state school resources may be illegal.
Personal use of computer communications is often viewed as desirable by organizations to motivate technology adoption.
Distinguishing between legitimate and illegitimate personal development in computing is difficult.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the distinction between commercial and personal use of university computing resources. He argues that while restrictions on commercial gain are standard, blanket prohibitions on non-commercial personal use are often impractical and counterproductive to learning. He suggests a quota or time-based system for 'free' CPU usage rather than total prohibition.
classification.title: Which Rights?

notable_claims: Institutions use account registration forms to force users to waive privacy rights regarding file searches and account termination.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the necessity of an appeals process for institutional rules and argues that students and faculty should participate in policy formulation. He specifically criticizes the practice of requiring users to sign waivers granting institutions unrestricted access to their files as a condition for obtaining computer accounts.
classification.title: Which Rights?
